skill1.description: You should be comfortable adding, subtracting, and multiplying positive and negative numbers

skill2.title: Order of Operations
skill2.description: Know how to follow PEMDAS (Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division, Addition/Subtraction)

skill3.title: Understanding Variables
skill3.description: Recognize that letters like x, y, and z can represent unknown numbers

algebraic.title: What is an Algebraic Expression?
algebraic.intro: An algebraic expression is a mathematical phrase that can contain numbers, variables, and operation symbols (+, −, ×, ÷).
algebraic.analogy: Think of expressions as mathematical sentences—just like regular sentences have words, mathematical expressions have numbers and variables!

terms.title: Terms in an Expression
terms.intro: A term is a single number, variable, or the product of numbers and variables separated by + or − signs.

coefficient.title: Coefficient
coefficient.intro: The coefficient is the numerical part of a term that contains a variable.

likeTerms.title: Like Terms
likeTerms.intro: Like terms are terms that have the same variables raised to the same powers. Only like terms can be combined.

combining.title: Combining Like Terms
combining.intro: To simplify expressions, combine like terms by adding or subtracting their coefficients. It's like organizing your closet—group similar items together!

distributive.title: Distributive Property
distributive.explanation: Multiply the term outside the parentheses by each term inside.

evaluating.title: Evaluating Expressions
evaluating.intro: To evaluate an expression means to find its value by substituting a number for the variable and calculating the result.

variables.title: Understanding Components
variables.caption: Variables change, constants stay the same

likeTerms.title: Identifying Like Terms
likeTerms.caption: Same variable and same exponent = like terms
likeTerms.reason1: All have variable x with exponent 1
likeTerms.reason2: All have y² (same variable, same exponent)

combining.title: Combining Like Terms Example
combining.caption: Group like terms and add/subtract coefficients

example1.title: Combining Like Terms
example1.question: Simplify: 4x + 5x - 3
example1.step1: Identify like terms: 4x and 5x are like terms

mistake1.title: Combining Unlike Terms
mistake1.wrong: Students try to combine 3x and 2x², thinking they can add them:
mistake1.correct: Remember: Only like terms can be combined. These have different exponents!
mistake1.explanation: 3x has exponent 1, while 2x² has exponent 2. They're as different as apples and oranges—you can't add them together!
mistake1.tip: Check the exponents! If they don't match exactly, don't combine the terms.

mistake2.title: Forgetting to Distribute the Negative
mistake2.wrong: When subtracting (4x + 3) - (2x + 1), students forget to distribute the negative:
mistake2.correct: The negative sign must be distributed to ALL terms in the parentheses:
mistake2.explanation: The minus sign is like multiplying by -1. It affects every term inside the parentheses, not just the first one!
mistake2.tip: Rewrite subtraction as adding a negative: (4x + 3) + (-1)(2x + 1)

mistake3.title: Not Distributing to All Terms
mistake3.wrong: When multiplying 3(x + 2), students might only multiply the first term:
mistake3.correct: The distributive property requires multiplying EVERY term inside:
mistake3.explanation: Think of it like handing out party favors—everyone inside the parentheses gets one! Every term must be multiplied by 3.

realWorld.title: Real World Applications
realWorld.intro: Algebraic expressions aren't just abstract math—they're powerful tools you'll use in everyday life!

app1.title: 💰 Shopping & Discounts
app1.description: Stores use algebraic expressions to calculate sale prices and discounts.
app1.example: A shirt costs $p. During a 20% off sale, you save 0.2p dollars. The final price is p - 0.2p = 0.8p dollars.

app2.title: 🌡️ Temperature Conversion
app2.description: Converting between Celsius and Fahrenheit uses an algebraic expression.
app2.example: To convert 25°C to Fahrenheit: F = (9/5) × 25 + 32 = 45 + 32 = 77°F. Scientists and weather forecasters use this daily!

app3.title: 🚗 Speed, Distance & Time
app3.description: Planning trips involves algebraic expressions relating speed, distance, and time.
app3.example: If you drive at 60 mph for t hours, the distance traveled is 60t miles. After 3 hours: d = 60 × 3 = 180 miles.

warmup.title: Warm-up Problems
warmup.description: Build your confidence with these easier problems!

practice.title: Practice Problems
practice.description: Master the core concepts with these exercises.

challenge.title: Challenge Problem
challenge.description: Ready to test your skills? This one's tougher!

exercise1.question: Which terms are like terms? 3x, 5y, 2x
exercise1.explanation: 3x and 2x are like terms because they have the same variable (x) with the same exponent.

exercise2.question: Evaluate 4x - 5 when x = 5. Enter your answer as a number.

exercise3.question: Simplify: 2x + 3x
exercise3.explanation: Combine coefficients: 2 + 3 = 5, so 2x + 3x = 5x. Remember: we add coefficients, not exponents!

exercise4.question: What is the coefficient in the term -7y? Enter the number (include the negative sign if needed).
exercise4.hint: The coefficient is the number in front of the variable, including its sign.
exercise4.explanation: The coefficient is -7. Don't forget the negative sign!

exercise5.question: Simplify using the distributive property: 5(2x - 3) + 4x
exercise5.explanation: First distribute: 5(2x) + 5(-3) + 4x = 10x - 15 + 4x. Then combine like terms: 14x - 15

notes.title: Tips & Tricks
notes.tip1: 📝 Only like terms can be combined. 2x + 3y cannot be simplified further because x and y are different variables.
notes.tip2: 🎯 When combining like terms, add or subtract only the coefficients—keep the variables the same! Think: 3 apples + 5 apples = 8 apples (not 8 apples²).
notes.tip3: 💡 The distributive property is your best friend: a(b + c) = ab + ac. It works forwards AND backwards!
notes.warning1: ⚠️ Don't confuse 3x and 3x²! They are NOT like terms because they have different exponents (1 vs 2).

conclusion.title: Excellent Work! 🎉
conclusion.summary: You've mastered algebraic expressions! Understanding variables, terms, coefficients, and how to simplify expressions is fundamental to all of algebra. These skills will be essential as you progress to solving equations and tackling more complex problems.
conclusion.takeaway1: Variables represent unknown values; constants are fixed numbers
conclusion.takeaway2: Like terms have the same variable with the same exponent
conclusion.takeaway3: Combine like terms by adding/subtracting coefficients only
conclusion.takeaway4: Use the distributive property: a(b + c) = ab + ac
